en: And rejoiced when pursuing the foe.
When swung in the dark of night,
It glowed red like an ember;
Only when sated with blood did it grow still,
And if not fully glutted with blood,
It quivered like hardened sinew,
While fury streamed from its face.
Its haft was wrapped in gold;
Without even fighting, it terrified the enemy.
Indeed, the magnanimous gray-maned hero
Had it fashioned to suit himself.
While this weapon was being made,
No small portion of the bloodthirsty hero’s treasury
Was consumed.
When the warrior raised it with a shout
And stood in all his menace,
Kongurbay, khan of Beijing,
And the khan of Kakan had recoiled.
Now that battle-axe of your bloodthirsty hero
Was in the hands of the infidel Kanchoro,
That ravager of nations,
That warrior in the fullness of his strength.
It hung ready upon his arm
As he surrounded and drove the vast black host of Jediger,
Pressing them onward in panic.
He made Köktelki, Köbösh Khan’s horse,
Prance proudly beneath him.
His courage was firm and his venom strong;
He threw every man he met into panic.
The flame issuing from his mouth
Was like the fire of a hand cannon;
The corners of his two eyes
Glowed like the embers of a vulture-lord.
His nose was like a swollen leather sack;
His tightly curled mustache
Was like a saber from Bukhara.
The fire burning in his two eyes
Was like a blaze flaming through a valley.
Kanchoro, calamity incarnate—
Such was his true might.
His two shoulders jutted high,
As though two giant black eagles perched upon them.
His two cheeks bulged,
Enough to feast two giants.
If he stirred, he seemed ready
To slaughter and drive off all the Kyrgyz.
When he barked out his cries,
His harsh, piercing voice
Was like a bolt of lightning.
None in the world could match his power;
He seemed ready to devour anyone who fought him.
His intention and design
Were to drive off and consume the Kyrgyz.
When the madman stirred,
He seemed already stained crimson,
His purpose firm as a mountain spur.
At Aichürök’s palace,
That accursed Kanchoro
Loosed his bow like pouring rain
And shot other arrows like hailstones.
The bowshots whistled,
The shafts curved through the air;
When they struck the palace,
Your sister-in-law despaired of life.
His army surged forward in turmoil;
To take the woman as plunder,
Kanchoro flooded in,
With greater numbers than before.
They raised fierce cries and clamor,
Playing drums and brass pipes;
They had the great drum sound the signal
And stunned all ears with its thunder.
At their center was a broad mountain ridge
Of warriors from many tribes.
At their head came
Kanchoro, the lionhearted hero.
The woman was alone, while they were countless—
How could her frail life not burn with anguish?
A roar rose before the gate;
When one listened to the herald’s voice,
He cried, “Kanchoro Khan!”
They loosed their bows like pouring rain
And fired their guns in volleys.
With Kanchoro Khan at their head,
They surrounded your sister-in-law at the gate
And steadily closed upon her.
When they entered the palace, he commanded:
“Seize the slave woman, seize her!
Bind her hands and feet;
Torment her and subdue her.
If she will not heed what she is told,
If she will not go where she is driven,
Stretch her out and beat her like a hide;
Keep striking her as punishment.
Put a felt cloak upon her,
Mount her on a barren mare,
Slash her soles and rub in salt,
Slash her fair face and fill the wounds with worms;
Then give her a writ of divorce
To take to her father Akun’s city,
And drive her off with her head hanging!
From her father Akun’s city
Did this shrew not come
Swaying in a fine fur coat,
Radiant upon an ambling bay horse?
Now let the disgraced wretch return in misery,
Flopping about on a barren mare.
If the hapless woman will not obey,
Seat her upon a bare wooden saddle,
Mount her on a gaunt mare,
Dress her in a filthy old robe,
And drive her off with her head bowed!
From her father Akun’s city
Did this shrew not come
Radiant in a silken robe,
Riding proudly on a gray pacer?
Now let the black-faced wretch return ruined
To the city of her father the khan,
Flopping about on a gaunt mare,
And drooping in a filthy old robe.
Let Akun’s people gossip about her
And together decide her fate.
With no brother-in-law to escort her,
No sister-in-law to receive a bridal gift,
They will say she flew away to marry,
That heaven-bound wonder amid grievous talk,
But lost that husband
And returned wandering and forlorn—
So shall Khan Akun’s people murmur.
Now let her do this instead;
Fulfill the word you gave.
Let us take moon-beautiful Aichürök
And make her our lady.
Fulfill your promise;
Stand by these words!
Your bloodthirsty husband is dead;
That gives a brave man grounds
To take his woman as wife—
Know that this is what has been said.
Before blood is spilled and a brave man dies,
Marry brave Kyyaz.
If you do not marry brave Kyyaz,
Your black hair, long as meadow grass,
Will be torn out strand by strand,
And today your head will be cut off.
Your mighty gray-maned hero is dead,
Your hands are bound,
And you have no answer left.
If you wish to live on without dying,
Heed what you are told
And go as senior wife
To Kyyaz, khan of the Jediger.
If you heed what is said
And go to brave Kyyaz,
Each day will be revelry, each day a game;
Know the weight of these words.
Your dwelling will be made of jewels;
Take both reins and the single bridle—
Full authority—from brave Kyyaz.
Let them call you chief among women;
Become the sovereign
Of the Jediger in the Seven Rivers.
Take off your widow’s garb, sister Aichürök;
Go with honor, without suffering humiliation,
Without letting others consume your gold,
And without being called a captive wife.
Go with your dignity intact.
You were a lionhearted tigress;
Heed what I tell you.
If you do not heed my words,
If you do not go to Kyyaz,
The hair on your crown will be ripped out,
Your precious head will be cut off,
Your words will go unheard,
Your two eyes will be gouged out,
Your body will be torn to pieces,
And all you say will be crushed!
Plundered and put to shame,
You yourself will be brought low.”
When Kanchoro said this,
Aichürök, daughter of Akun,
Had no choice but to hear him.
No child remained for her to cradle,
No descendant of the magnanimous hero;
Such filth, it seems, is this world.
As Kanchoro spoke,
She wished to die but could not,
Unable to take her own life.
The earth was too hard to enter,
Yet life was sweet when she wished to die;
She wailed, unable to stand,
Unable to surrender her fly-like soul.
The hapless slave with a hero’s form
Had no choice but to hear it.
Aichürök wept and mourned:
No male child remained behind her.
At that moment Aichürök,
Your poor heroine of manly stature,
Grew wrathful and grim;
The blood drained from her downcast face.
She pondered but could find no counsel;
The faithless world had overturned,
And she could find no bearings.
She clenched her teeth and summoned her courage,
Thinking, “If only I could find a way
To strike off the head of one of them—
Kanchoro Khan or Kyyaz Khan!
If only these men came near,
These villains who ravaged the people,
I would seize one and rip open his belly,
And swallow the black blood within
To quench my thirst.
If only I could tear one apart and slaughter him,
Drink his blood like kumiss,
And glut myself upon it;
Then my burning heart might be soothed,
My dimmed eyes might open,
All my anguish might scatter,
And my brow brighten like a mirror—
That would fulfill my desire.
If only I could bring greater havoc
Upon Kanchoro Khan and Kyyaz!”
So thought the warrior woman Aichürök,
That extraordinary, wrathful woman.
But the thought came to her too late:
If she met them, she would take their heads,
Bring grievous misery upon them,
Strike when they came near,
Count their vile lives as nothing,
And sever their heads with her sword.
Even if it meant her death,
Dear sister-in-law had reached
A resolve from which she would not retreat.
She was ready to fight them to the death;
The poor woman braced herself
To sacrifice her fly-like soul.
When she saw the tyrant khans,
The indomitable woman Aichürök
Coiled like a striking snake,
But there were no Argyn or Kyrgyz warriors
To break through and rescue her.
Your sister-in-law contemplated true battle,
But many wrestlers surrounded her.
Alone and suffering,
This woman bore endless sorrow;
Many champions encircled her.
Your heroic sister-in-law Aichürök
Was about to unleash a mighty conflict.
She spoke softly, yet firmly,
The moon-faced lady, in anguish,
And to brave Kyyaz and Kanchoro,
To those two she began to speak:
“Panther born of a mongrel,
Brave Kyyaz, born of a raven,
How can I take you as my ‘companion’?
How can I overcome my grief,
